questions.q: Which question is most likely to get useful facts from an AP clerk?
options: Would you use a tool that explains exceptions?
How do you usually handle exceptions?
Walk me through the last invoice exception you handled.
How much time would an AI tool save you?
Isn't it frustrating to chase buyers?
questions.why: Asking about a specific recent case gets real details, real systems and real time spent.

questions.q: A user says 'we always have to chase the buyer'. What should you do next?
options: Ask about the last time it happened
Write down 'always' as a fact
Show them your planned solution
Move to the next topic since it is clear
Ask how much a fix would be worth to them
questions.why: When someone says always or usually, ask for the last real case to get checkable facts.

questions.q: Which question is NOT leading?
options: Isn't it frustrating to chase buyers by email?
Wouldn't it be easier if approvals were automatic?
Don't you think the ERP is hard to use?
What happens after you email the buyer?
questions.why: A leading question hints at the answer you want; an open question about what happens does not.

questions.q: In your interview notes you write 'Waiting on buyer may be most of elapsed time'. How should this line be marked?
options: As a fact, since the clerk implied it
As your own interpretation, kept apart from facts and quotes
As a quote from the clerk
It should not be written down at all
questions.why: Keeping interpretations separate lets you later tell what was said from what you concluded.

questions.q: A clerk says exceptions take about ten minutes, but the event log shows cases open for several days. What explains this?
options: The clerk is wrong and the log is right
Ten minutes is touch time; days is elapsed time spent waiting
The log timestamps are in the wrong time zone
The log is wrong and the clerk is right
questions.why: Touch time is active work while elapsed time includes waiting, and both can be true.

questions.q: What are the three minimum fields an event log needs?
options: Case ID, user name and password
Activity name, cost and owner
Timestamp, department and SOP version
Case ID, activity name and timestamp
questions.why: With case ID, activity and timestamp you can compute elapsed time, rework and paths.

questions.q: The SOP requires a manager approval step, but the logs show it is often skipped. What do you do?
options: Raise it with the team without blame and ask whether it matches what they see
Report the team to compliance
Ignore the logs and map the SOP
Assume the logs are broken
Delete the step from your notes
questions.why: Disagreement between documents and logs is a finding, and the team's explanation reveals the real rule.

questions.q: On a swimlane map, why do lines that cross between lanes matter?
options: They show where the process ends
They mark steps that can be deleted
Each crossing is a handoff, where delay and errors collect
They show which steps are automated
questions.why: Every lane crossing is a handoff, and handoffs are where delay and errors collect.

questions.q: In BPMN, how do you show an email sent from the client company to an outside supplier?
options: A sequence flow (solid arrow) inside a lane
An exclusive gateway (diamond)
An end event (thick circle)
A message flow (dashed arrow) between pools
A new lane inside the client pool
questions.why: Message flows show communication between pools; sequence flows show order inside a pool.

questions.q: The process has many exceptions. In what order should you draw them?
options: Draw every exception first so nothing is missed
Draw the happy path first, then add the exceptions
Draw only the exceptions, since that is where pain is
Draw the future state first, then the exceptions
questions.why: Starting with every exception makes the map unreadable before anyone understands the main flow.

questions.q: The sponsor wants to see the future state map in week one. The current state has not been agreed. What do you do?
options: Draw the future state from the SOP
Skip the current state since it is changing
Get the current state agreed first, then draw the future state
Draw both at once to save time
questions.why: The future state should show exactly what changes, which only works once the current state is right.

questions.q: A RACI row for 'Approve pilot go-live' has two people marked A. What is the problem?
options: If two people are accountable, nobody is; each row needs exactly one A
Nothing, more owners means more support
There should be no A on approval rows
It should have two Rs instead
A can only be the FDE
questions.why: Exactly one A per row; two means unclear ownership and none means the decision drifts.

questions.q: What is the difference between C and I in a RACI?
options: C gives input before the decision (two-way); I is told after (one-way)
C does the work; I signs off
C is told after; I gives input before
C and I mean the same thing
questions.why: Consulted is a two-way input before the decision; Informed is one-way after it.

questions.q: Your PoC will send invoice data to an outside LLM API. When should you involve security?
options: The week before the pilot
Only if they ask
In the first two weeks, with a short note on what data goes where
After go-live, once results are proven
Never, IT covers security
questions.why: Finding security rules in week one costs a day; finding them in week eight can cost the pilot.

questions.q: Which acceptance criterion is testable?
options: The assistant is accurate
On the 50-case evaluation set, the stated cause matches the AP lead in at least 45 cases
The summaries are good
Users like the tool
The AI understands the exceptions
questions.why: Criteria must be specific enough that two people would agree whether they pass.

questions.q: Which part of the one-page brief prevents the most disputes later?
options: The title
The risks and assumptions
The data and systems list
The out-of-scope list
questions.why: Stating what will not be done stops people assuming it will be; read it out loud at sign-off.

questions.q: The team wants to pick the evaluation cases after seeing the first results. Why is that a problem?
options: It makes the set too large to run
Cases chosen later are always too easy to label
The test is no longer fair; agree how the set is built before building
Evaluation sets must be picked by the FDE alone
questions.why: Choosing cases after seeing results biases the test; a fixed rule such as every case from a recent week keeps it fair.

questions.q: Two experienced clerks barely use the new assistant. They know the causes already and say the tool slows them down. Which ADKAR stage is missing?
options: Awareness
Knowledge
Reinforcement
Desire
Ability
questions.why: They know why and how to change but do not want to, so Desire is the first stage they have not reached.

questions.q: Usage spiked after training but has fallen each week since, and the old spreadsheet is still in use. What should you do?
options: Find which ADKAR stage is missing and talk to two users about their last real case with the tool
Run the same training again for everyone
Ask the sponsor to make use mandatory
Add five new features to win users back
questions.why: These are failing signs, so go back to ADKAR to find the gap and hear from users directly.

questions.q: Where should the assistant appear to help adoption?
options: In a separate new window they must remember to open
Inside the screen people already use, such as the ERP or ticket view
Only in a weekly email report
On the FDE's laptop during office hours
questions.why: Putting the tool where people already work removes a step and helps it become part of the routine.
